newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - EMU tensions leave core Europe dazed.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - EMU tensions leave core Europe dazed.

text.p: Rising yields in core European bond markets will drive convergence trades near term, as the furore over Germany's plans to revalue Bundesbank gold prompts a dramatic reassessment of monetary union, analysts said.
Investors running for cover should avoid all markets embroiled in European Monetary Union (EMU) troubles and head for the safe-havens of gilts and U.S. Treasuries, they added.
"I think we're going to get more convergence trades, but from Bund yields rising not others coming down," said Bronwyn Curtis, chief economists at Nomura International here.
The single currency process has been dealt a double whammy this week by upheaval in its two staunchest supporters.

Germany's powerful Bundesbank sparked a very public row with the government after it rejected Bonn's plans to revalue its assets in a bid to bolster its finances for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
The government plans to go ahead anyway.
And all against the backdrop of political upheaval in France and the unsettling prospect of a left-wing, less euro friendly government waiting in the wings.
Curtis said it all added up to Bund yields rising by around 25 to 50 basis points.
"Clearly this is a real sea change in terms of Europe and Germany...It increases the chances of a broad EMU," she said.

So investors determined to see through the rough times should head for the high-yielders, said Curtis, adding Italy would likely be the best bet, and Spain too, although Bonos have already enjoyed a large degree of conversion.

David Brickman, European economist at Yamaichi International here, agreed the present EMU ructions should ultimately benefit the high yielders, but in the short term, they were vulnerable to a set-back as talk of a delay rather than a soft euro dominates.
Brickman said the final round of French elections on Sunday had far more implications for convergence trades than the Bundesbank-Bonn feud.
He said the fact the government said it intended to use any cash from gold revaluation to plug its debt, not its deficit, was crucial.

"If that is the case then it won't have any impact whatsoever on German qualification for Maastricht," he said. "It was widely accepted in the EU that Germany was going to be pardoned on its debt anyway because of unification."
A win for the combined left in Sunday's second round of French elections on the other hand would raise huge question marks over the timetable for EMU and the strength of the euro.
So in the meantime, the best advice from strategists was to give EMU countries the cold shoulder altogether.
Gilts have emerged as a popular alternative.
Michael Burke, bond strategist at Citibank here, said the 10-year gilt/Bund spread could get down as far as 100 basis points by the end of the year. By 1030 GMT it stood at 140 basis points.
He said while high yielding European economies may prove a good buy in the end, the present risk-reward ratio gave no incentive to jump in now.

Curtis agreed gilts and U.S. Treasuries looked attractive. But she said looming U.S. non-farm payrolls data may prompt a widening of the Treasury/Bund spread near term back towards 100 basis points, before it narrows to around 75 basis points and less in the coming year. Half way through Thursday, that spread was at 92.
